01-General-Thinking/first-principles.md:
References

Attributed to Aristotle, who described first principles as the foundational axioms from which knowledge is derived. René Descartes systematized the method in philosophy; it was reinvigorated in engineering practice by figures such as Richard Feynman.

  • Discourse on the Method — René Descartes (1637)
  • The Feynman Lectures on Physics — Richard P. Feynman, Robert B. Leighton & Matthew Sands (1963)
  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
01-General-Thinking/inversion.md:
References

Formalized as a mathematical strategy by Carl Jacobi (19th century), who advised "man muss immer umkehren" (always invert). Popularized as a general thinking tool by Charlie Munger.

  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
  • The Art of Thinking Clearly — Rolf Dobelli (2011)
01-General-Thinking/second-order-effects:
References

Articulated in investor practice by Howard Marks and Charlie Munger; the underlying systems-level idea was developed rigorously by Donella Meadows in systems dynamics.

  • The Most Important Thing — Howard Marks (2011)
  • Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows (2008)
  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
01-General-Thinking/occams-razor.md:
References

William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), English friar and logician. The principle — that entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity — was named and formalized in the 19th century.

  • The Logic of Scientific Discovery — Karl Popper (1934)
  • The Demon-Haunted World — Carl Sagan (1996)
01-General-Thinking/hanlons-razor.md:
References

Named after Robert J. Hanlon, who submitted the aphorism to a 1980 joke book. Variant forms appear in writings attributed to Napoleon Bonaparte and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

  • The Art of Thinking Clearly — Rolf Dobelli (2011)
  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
01-General-Thinking/circle-of-competence:
References

Developed and named by Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger in Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters, beginning in the early 1990s.

  • The Essays of Warren Buffett — Warren Buffett, ed. Lawrence Cunningham (1997)
  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
01-General-Thinking/map-territory.md:
References

Alfred Korzybski introduced the phrase "the map is not the territory" in a 1931 address to the American Mathematical Society, elaborated in his general semantics framework.

  • Science and Sanity — Alfred Korzybski (1933)
  • The Black Swan — Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2007)
01-General-Thinking/probabilistic-thinki:
References

Rooted in the probability theory of Pierre-Simon Laplace and Thomas Bayes (18th century). Applied to everyday decision-making by Annie Duke and Nate Silver.

  • Thinking in Bets — Annie Duke (2018)
  • The Signal and the Noise — Nate Silver (2012)
  • Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk — Peter L. Bernstein (1996)
01-General-Thinking/thought-experiment.m:
References

Central to the natural philosophy of Galileo Galilei (17th century) and formalized in physics by Ernst Mach and Albert Einstein, who called them Gedankenexperimente.

  • Einstein: His Life and Universe — Walter Isaacson (2007)
  • Thirty Years that Shook Physics — George Gamow (1966)
01-General-Thinking/socratic-thinking.md:
References

Developed by Socrates (470–399 BC) and documented by his student Plato in the Dialogues. The method of disciplined questioning was revived in modern pedagogy by Leonard Nelson and Richard Paul.

  • The Republic — Plato (trans. Benjamin Jowett, c. 380 BC)
  • Socratic Seminars in the Block — Wanda H. Ball & Pam Brewer (1996)
01-General-Thinking/pre-mortem.md:
References

Developed by psychologist Gary Klein and introduced in a 1989 paper. Popularized in business and decision-making by Daniel Kahneman.

  • Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions — Gary Klein (1998)
  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
01-General-Thinking/post-mortem.md:
References

Borrowed from medical autopsy practice; systematized in engineering and software through disciplines such as blameless post-mortems (originated at Google SRE). Popularized in business by Ben Horowitz.

  • The Hard Thing About Hard Things — Ben Horowitz (2014)
  • Site Reliability Engineering — Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff & Niall Richard Murphy (2016)

Developed and popularized by Nassim Nicholas Taleb, who built the concept of convex payoffs as a cornerstone of his philosophical framework across the Incerto series.

  • The Black Swan — Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2007)
  • Antifragile — Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2012)
01-General-Thinking/de-bonos-six-thinkin:
References

Created by Edward de Bono and introduced in his 1985 book. De Bono also originated the concept of lateral thinking.

  • Six Thinking Hats — Edward de Bono (1985)
  • Lateral Thinking — Edward de Bono (1970)
References

Created by organizational theorist Chris Argyris in the 1970s; widely disseminated by Peter Senge, who included it in The Fifth Discipline.

  • Overcoming Organizational Defenses — Chris Argyris (1990)
  • The Fifth Discipline — Peter M. Senge (1990)
01-General-Thinking/regret-minimization-:
References

Articulated by Jeff Bezos in 1997 as the personal heuristic he used when deciding to leave a hedge fund job to start Amazon.

  • Invent and Wander: The Collected Writings of Jeff Bezos — Jeff Bezos, ed. Walter Isaacson (2021)
  • The Everything Store — Brad Stone (2013)
01-General-Thinking/two-way-doors.md:
References

Introduced by Jeff Bezos in Amazon's 2015 annual shareholder letter as a framework for distinguishing reversible from irreversible decisions.

  • Invent and Wander: The Collected Writings of Jeff Bezos — Jeff Bezos, ed. Walter Isaacson (2021)
  • Working Backwards — Colin Bryar & Bill Carr (2021)
02-Systems/feedback-loops.md:
References

Formalized by Norbert Wiener in cybernetics (1948) and by Jay Forrester in system dynamics (1950s). Donella Meadows made the concept accessible to non-technical audiences.

  • Cybernetics — Norbert Wiener (1948)
  • Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows (2008)
02-Systems/bottlenecks.md:
References

Rigorously formalized as the Theory of Constraints by Eliyahu M. Goldratt in the early 1980s, introduced to a mass audience through his novel The Goal.

  • The Goal — Eliyahu M. Goldratt & Jeff Cox (1984)
  • The Phoenix Project — Gene Kim, Kevin Behr & George Spafford (2013)
02-Systems/emergence.md:
References

The term was coined by philosopher G. H. Lewes (1875). The modern scientific framework was developed by Philip Anderson (“More is Different,” 1972) and popularized by Steven Johnson.

  • Emergence: The Connected Lives of Ants, Brains, Cities, and Software — Steven Johnson (2001)
  • Complex Adaptive Systems — John H. Miller & Scott E. Page (2007)
02-Systems/equilibrium.md:
References

General equilibrium theory was developed by Léon Walras (1874). Game-theoretic equilibrium was formalized by John Nash (1950). John Maynard Keynes examined dynamic disequilibrium.

  • Elements of Pure Economics — Léon Walras (1874)
  • A Beautiful Mind — Sylvia Nasar (1998)
02-Systems/scale.md:
References

Biological scaling laws were formalized by Max Kleiber (1932). The unifying framework across organisms, cities, and companies was developed by Geoffrey West at the Santa Fe Institute.

  • Scale — Geoffrey West (2017)
  • The Long Tail — Chris Anderson (2006)
02-Systems/critical-mass.md:
References

The concept of tipping points and critical mass was formalized in social science by Thomas Schelling (1971) and in diffusion research by Everett Rogers.

  • Diffusion of Innovations — Everett M. Rogers (1962; 5th ed. 2003)
  • The Tipping Point — Malcolm Gladwell (2000)
02-Systems/diminishing-returns.md:
References

Independently described by Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot (1767) and formalized in economics by David Ricardo in his theory of rent (1817).

  • Principles of Political Economy and Taxation — David Ricardo (1817)
  • Economics — Paul A. Samuelson (1948)
02-Systems/margin-of-safety.md:
References

Developed by Benjamin Graham as a cornerstone of value investing, first articulated in Security Analysis (1934) and made accessible in The Intelligent Investor.

  • The Intelligent Investor — Benjamin Graham (1949)
  • Security Analysis — Benjamin Graham & David L. Dodd (1934)
02-Systems/churn.md:
References

Emerged as a key SaaS business metric in the late 1990s–2000s. David Skok and Bill Gurley were among the earliest investors to publish rigorous frameworks for its interpretation.

  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)
  • Crossing the Chasm — Geoffrey A. Moore (1991)
02-Systems/algorithms.md:
References

The formal theory of algorithms was established by Alan Turing (1936) and Alonzo Church. Donald Knuth produced the definitive reference work beginning in 1968.

  • The Art of Computer Programming (Vol. 1) — Donald E. Knuth (1968)
  • Algorithms to Live By — Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths (2016)
02-Systems/irreducibility.md:
References

The mathematical limits of formal systems were proved by Kurt Gödel (1931, incompleteness theorems) and Alan Turing (1936, halting problem). Gregory Chaitin extended the work into algorithmic information theory.

  • Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid — Douglas R. Hofstadter (1979)
  • The Emperor's New Mind — Roger Penrose (1989)
02-Systems/conways-law.md:
References

Proposed by computer programmer Melvin Conway in a 1968 article in Datamation. Fred Brooks observed related effects in The Mythical Man-Month; the empirical case was strengthened by Nicole Forsgren et al.

  • The Mythical Man-Month — Frederick P. Brooks Jr. (1975)
  • Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps — Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble & Gene Kim (2018)
02-Systems/red-queen-dilemma.md:
References

Named for the Red Queen's remark in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871). Formalized as an evolutionary hypothesis by Leigh Van Valen (1973); applied to business by Andy Grove.

  • The Red Queen: Sex and the Evolution of Human Nature — Matt Ridley (1993)
  • Only the Paranoid Survive — Andrew S. Grove (1996)
03-Economics/trade-offs.md:
References

The concept of opportunity cost and trade-offs was systematized by classical economists including Adam Smith and David Ricardo. Frédéric Bastiat's broken-window parable (1850) is one of its most durable illustrations.

  • The Wealth of Nations — Adam Smith (1776)
  • Basic Economics — Thomas Sowell (2000)
03-Economics/scarcity.md:
References

Thomas Malthus established the foundational argument (1798). Lionel Robbins gave economics its canonical definition as "the science of scarcity" in 1932.

  • An Essay on the Principle of Population — Thomas Robert Malthus (1798)
  • An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science — Lionel Robbins (1932)
03-Economics/specialization.md:
References

Adam Smith's pin-factory analysis of the division of labour (1776) is the founding statement. David Ricardo extended it into international trade through comparative advantage (1817).

  • The Wealth of Nations — Adam Smith (1776)
  • Principles of Political Economy and Taxation — David Ricardo (1817)
03-Economics/optimization.md:
References

Mathematical optimization was developed by Leonhard Euler and Joseph-Louis Lagrange (18th century). Linear programming was formalized by George Dantzig (1947) and practical applications expanded by operations research.

  • Algorithms to Live By — Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths (2016)
  • How to Solve It — George Pólya (1945)
03-Economics/monopoly-vs-competition.md:
References

Adam Smith (1776) described monopoly power; Joan Robinson and Edward Chamberlin independently developed theories of imperfect competition (1933). Peter Thiel re-examined the topic from an entrepreneur's perspective.

  • Competition Demystified — Bruce Greenwald & Judd Kahn (2005)
  • Zero to One — Peter Thiel & Blake Masters (2014)
03-Economics/efficiency.md:
References

Vilfredo Pareto formalized allocative efficiency (1906). Frederick Winslow Taylor pioneered operational efficiency through scientific management (1911). These two traditions feed modern usage.

  • The Principles of Scientific Management — Frederick Winslow Taylor (1911)
  • The Goal — Eliyahu M. Goldratt & Jeff Cox (1984)
03-Economics/debt.md:
References

Economic analysis of debt crises was pioneered by Hyman Minsky (financial instability hypothesis) and documented historically by Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff.

  • This Time Is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly — Carmen Reinhart & Kenneth Rogoff (2009)
  • Stabilizing an Unstable Economy — Hyman P. Minsky (1986)
03-Economics/creative-destruction.md:
References

Coined and theorized by Joseph Schumpeter in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), drawing on Karl Marx's earlier observations about capitalism's self-transforming nature.

  • Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy — Joseph A. Schumpeter (1942)
  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
03-Economics/bubbles.md:
References

Charles Kindleberger produced the canonical historical taxonomy (1978). Robert Shiller applied behavioral economics to explain their persistence.

  • Manias, Panics, and Crashes — Charles P. Kindleberger (1978)
  • Irrational Exuberance — Robert J. Shiller (2000)
03-Economics/interdependence.md:
References

Interdependence as an economic organizing principle was described by Adam Smith and David Ricardo. Modern theories of complex interdependence were developed by Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye (1977).

  • The Wealth of Nations — Adam Smith (1776)
  • Power and Interdependence — Robert O. Keohane & Joseph S. Nye (1977)
03-Economics/greshams-law.md:
References

Named for Sir Thomas Gresham (16th century), who explained currency debasement to Queen Elizabeth I. The principle was named and generalized by Henry Dunning Macleod (1858).

  • The Ascent of Money — Niall Ferguson (2008)
  • Money: The Unauthorized Biography — Felix Martin (2013)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/leverage.md:
References

The physics of leverage was rigorously described by Archimedes (3rd century BC). Charlie Munger extended it as a mental model across financial and organizational contexts.

  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
  • The Feynman Lectures on Physics — Richard P. Feynman, Robert B. Leighton & Matthew Sands (1963)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/velocity.md:
References

Formalized by Isaac Newton in the Principia Mathematica (1687). As an organizational metaphor, applied widely in agile and lean frameworks.

  • Principia Mathematica — Isaac Newton (1687)
  • Thinking in Systems — Donella H. Meadows (2008)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/inertia.md:
References

Newton's First Law of Motion (1687). Applied to organizations by Clayton Christensen (innovator's dilemma) and to individual behavior by Daniel Kahneman (System 1 thinking).

  • Principia Mathematica — Isaac Newton (1687)
  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/friction.md:
References

Laws of friction were described by Guillaume Amontons (1699) and Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1781). Applied to user behavior and product design by Nir Eyal and BJ Fogg.

  • Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products — Nir Eyal (2014)
  • Nudge — Richard H. Thaler & Cass R. Sunstein (2008)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/activation-ener:
References

The Arrhenius equation formalizing activation energy was published by Svante Arrhenius in 1889. Applied to behavioral change by Chip Heath and Dan Heath.

  • Switch: How to Change Things When Change Is Hard — Chip Heath & Dan Heath (2010)
  • The Feynman Lectures on Physics — Richard P. Feynman, Robert B. Leighton & Matthew Sands (1963)

The laws were established by Sadi Carnot (1824), Rudolf Clausius (entropy and the Second Law, 1850), and Lord Kelvin. The concept of entropy has been extended into information theory by Claude Shannon (1948).

  • The Laws of Thermodynamics: A Very Short Introduction — Peter Atkins (2010)
  • A Mathematical Theory of Communication — Claude E. Shannon (1948)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/catalysts.md:
References

The concept of catalysis was named by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1835. Applied broadly to innovation and change management by Clayton Christensen and more recently by Matt Ridley.

  • How Innovation Works — Matt Ridley (2020)
  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/alloying.md:
References

Alloying has roots in Bronze Age metallurgy (c. 3000 BC). Its application as a strategy metaphor — combining complementary elements — draws on materials science literature popularized by Mark Miodownik.

  • Stuff Matters: Exploring the Marvelous Materials That Shape Our Man-Made World — Mark Miodownik (2013)
  • The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Civilization in the Aftermath of a Cataclysm — Lewis Dartnell (2014)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/reciprocity.md:
References

Reciprocity as a social and economic norm has deep anthropological roots. Robert Cialdini identified it as one of the six principles of influence in his landmark 1984 study.

  • Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion — Robert B. Cialdini (1984)
  • Presuasion — Robert B. Cialdini (2016)
04-Physics-and-Chemistry/relativity.md:
References

Albert Einstein published the Special Theory of Relativity in 1905 and the General Theory in 1915. The principle that observation depends on frame of reference has been applied in philosophy, economics, and design.

  • Einstein: His Life and Universe — Walter Isaacson (2007)
05-Psychology/incentives.md:
References

The role of incentives was foundational in Adam Smith's theory of markets (1776). Charlie Munger famously summarized the principle: 'Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome.'

  • Freakonomics — Steven D. Levitt & Stephen J. Dubner (2005)
05-Psychology/loss-aversion.md:
References

Identified and named by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in their Prospect Theory paper, one of the most cited articles in economics.

  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
  • Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics — Richard H. Thaler (2015)
05-Psychology/sunk-cost.md:
References

The sunk cost fallacy was formalized in behavioral economics by Richard Thaler (1980) and elaborated in Kahneman and Tversky's work on framing and loss aversion.

  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
  • Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics — Richard H. Thaler (2015)
05-Psychology/anchoring.md:
References

Discovered and named by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in their seminal 1974 paper 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases.'

  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)

05-Psychology/confirmation-bias.md:

Identified experimentally by Peter Wason in his 2-4-6 task (1960). Systematically reviewed by Raymond Nickerson (1998). Charlie Munger called it 'the most powerful' of cognitive biases.

05-Psychology/availability-bias.md:

Identified by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in their heuristics and biases program, first described in a 1973 paper.

Documented by David Dunning and Justin Kruger in a 1999 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, titled 'Unskilled and Unaware of It.'

References

Proposed by Abraham Maslow in a 1943 paper 'A Theory of Human Motivation,' published in Psychological Review, and elaborated in Motivation and Personality (1954).

References

Developed by David McClelland, who introduced the three motivational needs (achievement, affiliation, power) in The Achieving Society (1961) and refined the theory over subsequent decades.

Developed by Chilean economist Manfred Max-Neef and colleagues, introduced in Human Scale Development (1991) as a critique of GDP-centric development models.

05-Psychology/erg-theory.md:

Proposed by Clayton Alderfer as a revision and empirical refinement of Maslow's hierarchy, introduced in a 1969 paper in Psychological Review.

06-Startups/product-market-fit.md:
References

The term was coined by Andy Rachleff and popularized in a landmark 2007 blog post by Marc Andreessen, 'The Only Thing That Matters.'

  • Zero to One — Peter Thiel & Blake Masters (2014)
06-Startups/build-measure-learn.md:
References

Formalized by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup (2011), drawing on Toyota's production system and Steve Blank's customer development methodology.

  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)

06-Startups/mvp.md:
References

The term 'minimum viable product' was coined by Frank Robinson and popularized as a central concept by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup. Steve Blank's customer development work provided the empirical foundation.

  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)
  • The Four Steps to the Epiphany — Steve Blank (2003)
06-Startups/pivot-or-persevere.md:
References

Formalized by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup (2011) as a structured decision point in the Build-Measure-Learn loop.

  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)
  • Disciplined Entrepreneurship — Bill Aulet (2013)
06-Startups/customer-development.md:
References

Developed by Steve Blank, introduced in The Four Steps to the Epiphany (2003). The methodology became a foundation for the Lean Startup movement.

  • The Four Steps to the Epiphany — Steve Blank (2003)
  • The Startup Owner's Manual — Steve Blank & Bob Dorf (2012)
06-Startups/innovation-accounting.md:
References

Introduced by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup (2011) to provide a rigorous alternative to vanity metrics for measuring early-stage progress.

  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)
  • Measure What Matters — John Doerr (2018)
07-Business/business-model-canvas.md:
References

Developed by Alexander Osterwalder, based on his doctoral dissertation under Yves Pigneur. Introduced to a mass audience in Business Model Generation (2010).

  • Business Model Generation — Alexander Osterwalder & Yves Pigneur (2010)
  • Value Proposition Design — Alexander Osterwalder et al. (2014)
07-Business/value-prop-canvas.md:
References

Developed by Alexander Osterwalder as a companion tool to the Business Model Canvas, formalized in Value Proposition Design (2014).

  • Value Proposition Design — Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur, Greg Bernarda & Alan Smith (2014)
  • Business Model Generation — Alexander Osterwalder & Yves Pigneur (2010)
07-Business/innovation-funnel.md:
References

The stage-gate process — the formal predecessor — was developed by Robert G. Cooper in the 1980s. The funnel metaphor was widely adopted in corporate innovation programs.

  • Winning at New Products — Robert G. Cooper (1986)
  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
07-Business/portfolio-map.md:
References

The BCG Growth-Share Matrix was created by Bruce Henderson at the Boston Consulting Group in 1970. Variants (GE-McKinsey, Ansoff Matrix) extended the concept.

  • Perspectives on Experience — Boston Consulting Group (1968)
  • Good Strategy Bad Strategy — Richard Rumelt (2011)
07-Business/experiment-design.md:
References

The formal theory of designed experiments was established by Ronald A. Fisher in The Design of Experiments (1935). Applied to online products by Ron Kohavi and colleagues at Microsoft.

  • The Design of Experiments — Ronald A. Fisher (1935)
  • Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments — Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu (2020)
07-Business/assumption-mapping.md:
References

Developed by David Bland and Alexander Osterwalder as a structured pre-experiment tool, introduced in Testing Business Ideas (2019).

  • Testing Business Ideas — David J. Bland & Alexander Osterwalder (2019)
  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)
07-Business/stakeholder-mapping-salience:
References

Stakeholder theory was foundational work by R. Edward Freeman (1984). The salience model (power, legitimacy, urgency) was developed by Ronald Mitchell, Bradley Agle, and Donna Wood (1997).

  • Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach — R. Edward Freeman (1984)
  • Toward a Theory of Stakeholder Identification and Salience — Ronald K. Mitchell, Bradley R. Agle & Donna J. Wood — Academy of Management Review, Vol. 22, No. 4 (1997)
08-Mathematics/compounding.md:
References

Compound interest was mathematically formalized by Jacob Bernoulli (1683, continuous compounding). Warren Buffett has long described compounding as the foundational principle of his investment philosophy.

  • The Snowball: Warren Buffett and the Business of Life — Alice Schroeder (2008)
  • The Psychology of Money — Morgan Housel (2020)
08-Mathematics/local-maxima.md:
References

Local maxima arise in calculus and optimization theory (Leibniz, Newton, 17th century). Applied to product strategy and exploration by Brian Christian and Tom Griffiths.

  • Algorithms to Live By — Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths (2016)
  • How to Solve It — George Pólya (1945)
08-Mathematics/regression-to-the-mean.md:
References

Discovered by Francis Galton in his study of hereditary height (1886), who called it 'regression towards mediocrity.' Daniel Kahneman identified it as one of the most underappreciated statistical phenomena in decision-making.

  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
  • The Mismeasure of Man — Stephen Jay Gould (1981)
08-Mathematics/randomness.md:
References

Probability theory was developed by Pascal, Fermat, Laplace, and Gauss. Nassim Nicholas Taleb applied the concept to the systematic underestimation of randomness in human affairs.

  • Fooled by Randomness — Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2001)
  • The Drunkard's Walk: How Randomness Rules Our Lives — Leonard Mlodinow (2008)
08-Mathematics/sampling.md:
References

Statistical sampling theory was developed by William Gosset ('Student,' 1908) and Ronald Fisher (1920s). Survey sampling was formalized by Jerzy Neyman (1934).

  • The Lady Tasting Tea: How Statistics Revolutionized Science — David Salsburg (2001)
  • How to Lie with Statistics — Darrell Huff (1954)
08-Mathematics/surface-area.md:
References

Surface area principles derive from classical geometry. Applied to risk, opportunity, and organizational exposure as a metaphor developed across business and security literature.

  • Scale — Geoffrey West (2017)
  • Antifragile — Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2012)
08-Mathematics/multiply-by-zero.md:
References

The algebraic property is ancient. As a business and leadership principle — that a single fatal weakness nullifies all strengths — it was articulated by Patrick Lencioni and Jim Collins.

  • Good to Great — Jim Collins (2001)
  • The Five Dysfunctions of a Team — Patrick Lencioni (2002)
09-Network-Effects/network-effects.md:
References

The value of telephone networks was noted by Theodore Vail (AT&T president, 1908). Metcalfe's Law (network value scales with n²) was formulated by Robert Metcalfe (1980). Andrew Chen produced the most comprehensive modern taxonomy.

  • The Cold Start Problem — Andrew Chen (2021)
  • Platform Revolution — Geoffrey G. Parker, Marshall W. Van Alstyne & Sangeet Paul Choudary (2016)
09-Network-Effects/viral-growth.md:
References

The epidemiological concept of R0 was adapted for product growth by Andrew Chen ('The Law of Shitty Clickthroughs,' 2007 et al.) and formalized in the viral coefficient model.

  • The Cold Start Problem — Andrew Chen (2021)
  • Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products — Nir Eyal (2014)
09-Network-Effects/marketplace.md:
References

The economics of two-sided markets was formalized by Jean Tirole and Jean-Charles Rochet in a 2003 paper. Platform strategy was synthesized by Parker, Van Alstyne, and Choudary.

  • Platform Revolution — Geoffrey G. Parker, Marshall W. Van Alstyne & Sangeet Paul Choudary (2016)
  • The Cold Start Problem — Andrew Chen (2021)
09-Network-Effects/defensibility.md:
References

Competitive advantage and industry structure were analyzed by Michael Porter (1979, 1985). Warren Buffett popularized the 'moat' metaphor; Pat Dorsey synthesized it for investors.

  • Competitive Advantage — Michael E. Porter (1985)
  • The Little Book That Builds Wealth — Pat Dorsey (2008)
10-Learning/model-chaining.md:
References

Developed as a practice by Charlie Munger, who described 'the lollapalooza effect' of multiple models converging on the same conclusion. Shane Parrish systematized it through Farnam Street.

  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
  • The Great Mental Models (Vol. 1) — Shane Parrish (2019)
10-Learning/t-shaped.md:
References

The T-shaped professional concept was popularized by Tim Brown of IDEO (c. 2005–2009) and has roots in David Guest's 1991 article in The Guardian on the versatile professional.

  • Change by Design — Tim Brown (2009)
  • Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World — David Epstein (2019)
10-Learning/five-hour-rule.md:
References

Attributed in spirit to Benjamin Franklin's lifelong habit of deliberate reading and reflection. Articulated as a rule by Michael Simmons in a 2016 Medium article.

  • Deep Work — Cal Newport (2016)
  • Mastery — Robert Greene (2012)
10-Learning/learning-transfer.md:
References

Studied by Edward Thorndike and Robert Woodworth in 1901 (identical elements theory). Modern research was advanced by Robert Haskell and, in applied learning science, by Peter Brown, Henry Roediger, and Mark McDaniel.

  • Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning — Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III & Mark A. McDaniel (2014)
  • Transfer of Learning: Cognition, Instruction, and Reasoning — Robert E. Haskell (2001)
11-Art/audience.md:
References

Rhetoric — the art of adapting communication to audience — was systematized by Aristotle in Rhetoric (c. 350 BC). Modern applied communication research builds on this foundation.

  • Rhetoric — Aristotle (c. 350 BC)
  • Made to Stick — Chip Heath & Dan Heath (2007)
11-Art/framing.md:
References

Sociological framing theory was developed by Erving Goffman (1974). Kahneman and Tversky demonstrated framing effects in decision-making in a landmark 1981 paper.

  • Frame Analysis — Erving Goffman (1974)
  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
11-Art/contrast.md:
References

The role of contrast in perception was analyzed by Rudolf Arnheim in Art and Visual Perception (1954). Applied to communication by Chip Heath and Dan Heath.

  • Art and Visual Perception — Rudolf Arnheim (1954)
  • Made to Stick — Chip Heath & Dan Heath (2007)
11-Art/rhythm.md:
References

Rhythm as a structural element of composition was analyzed by Aristotle in Poetics (c. 335 BC). Modern prose rhythm was examined by Strunk and White and by Francis-Noël Thomas and Mark Turner.

  • The Elements of Style — William Strunk Jr. & E.B. White (1959)
  • Clear and Simple as the Truth — Francis-Noël Thomas & Mark Turner (1994)
12-Pre-built-Chains/pricing-decision.md:
References

This pre-built chain synthesizes concepts from multiple fields including economics (price theory), psychology (anchoring, loss aversion), and strategy (competitive positioning). No single originator; draws on the framework authors listed throughout this collection.

  • Priceless: The Myth of Fair Value — William Poundstone (2010)
  • The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing — Thomas T. Nagle & Georg Müller (2018)
12-Pre-built-Chains/market-entry.md:
References

Market entry strategy synthesizes Michael Porter's Five Forces, Clayton Christensen's disruption theory, and Geoffrey Moore's adoption lifecycle. No single originator.

  • Competitive Strategy — Michael E. Porter (1980)
  • Crossing the Chasm — Geoffrey A. Moore (1991)
12-Pre-built-Chains/hiring-decision.md:
References

Structured hiring research was pioneered by Frank Schmidt and John Hunter (1998 meta-analysis on predictors of job performance). Laszlo Bock synthesized it in the context of knowledge work.

  • Work Rules! — Laszlo Bock (2015)
  • Who: The A Method for Hiring — Geoff Smart & Randy Street (2008)
12-Pre-built-Chains/product-launch.md:
References

Product launch frameworks synthesize Geoffrey Moore's adoption curve, Eric Ries's Build-Measure-Learn, and Al Ries and Jack Trout's positioning work. No single originator.

  • Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind — Al Ries & Jack Trout (1981)
  • Crossing the Chasm — Geoffrey A. Moore (1991)
References

Investment decision frameworks draw on Benjamin Graham's value investing framework and Charlie Munger's multi-model approach. No single originator; synthesizes multiple concepts in this collection.

  • The Intelligent Investor — Benjamin Graham (1949)
  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
12-Pre-built-Chains/should-i-quit.md:
References

Decision frameworks for quitting synthesize Daniel Kahneman's work on sunk costs and loss aversion, Seth Godin's strategic quitting analysis, and Jeff Bezos's regret minimization framework.

  • The Dip: A Little Book That Teaches You When to Quit — Seth Godin (2007)
  • Thinking in Bets — Annie Duke (2018)
12-Pre-built-Chains/life-decision.md:
References

Life decision frameworks synthesize Clayton Christensen's application of business strategy to personal choices, Jeff Bezos's regret minimization, and Kahneman's work on decision quality.

  • How Will You Measure Your Life? — Clayton M. Christensen, James Allworth & Karen Dillon (2012)
  • Thinking in Bets — Annie Duke (2018)
05-Psychology/trust.md:
References

Trust as a social and economic concept was studied by Francis Fukuyama (1995) and Robert Putnam (social capital, 1993). Organizational trust research was advanced by Roger Mayer, James Davis, and David Schoorman (1995).

  • Trust: The Social Virtues and the Creation of Prosperity — Francis Fukuyama (1995)
  • The Speed of Trust — Stephen M. R. Covey & Rebecca R. Merrill (2006)
  • Bowling Alone — Robert D. Putnam (2000)
02-Systems/s-curves.md:
References

The logistic (S-curve) growth function was described by Pierre François Verhulst (1838). Applied to technology adoption by Everett Rogers (1962) and to competitive strategy by Richard Foster (1986) and Clayton Christensen.

  • Diffusion of Innovations — Everett M. Rogers (1962; 5th ed. 2003)
  • Innovation: The Attacker's Advantage — Richard N. Foster (1986)
  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
06-Startups/jobs-to-be-done.md:
References

The Jobs to Be Done framework was developed by Clayton Christensen, Bob Moesta, and Anthony Ulwick in the 1990s–2000s. Christensen's milkshake interview became the iconic illustration.

  • Competing Against Luck — Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon & David S. Duncan (2016)
  • Jobs to Be Done: Theory to Practice — Anthony W. Ulwick (2016)
  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
05-Psychology/psychological-safety.md:
References

The concept was introduced by Edgar Schein and Warren Bennis (1965) and rigorously studied by Amy Edmondson, whose 1999 paper on team learning remains the foundational reference.

  • The Fearless Organization — Amy C. Edmondson (2018)
  • Daring Greatly — Brené Brown (2012)
10-Learning/pre-built-chains.md:
References

The practice of chaining mental models — applying several sequentially to a decision — was developed by Charlie Munger, who described it as the source of 'lollapalooza effects.' This skill describes the meta-practice itself.

  • Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger, ed. Peter Kaufman (2005)
  • The Great Mental Models (Vol. 1) — Shane Parrish (2019)
01-General-Thinking/analogical-reasoning:
References

The cognitive science of analogy was formalized by Dedre Gentner in her structure-mapping theory (1983) and by Keith Holyoak and Paul Thagard. Its role in scientific discovery was documented by Kevin Dunbar.

  • Mental Leaps: Analogy in Creative Thought — Keith J. Holyoak & Paul Thagard (1995)
  • The Analogical Mind — Dedre Gentner, Keith J. Holyoak & Boicho N. Kokinov, eds. (2001)
01-General-Thinking/divergent-and-conver:
References

Divergent thinking was identified and named by J.P. Guilford in his 1956 presidential address to the American Psychological Association. Convergent thinking as the complementary mode was developed in creativity research by Guilford and later by Edward de Bono.

  • The Creative Mind: Myths and Mechanisms — Margaret A. Boden (2004)
  • A Whack on the Side of the Head — Roger von Oech (1983)
02-Systems/exploration-vs-exploitation.m:
References

Formalized in organizational learning by James March in a landmark 1991 paper in Organization Science. The underlying tension appears in multi-armed bandit problems in statistics, studied by Herbert Robbins (1952).

  • Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning — James G. March — Organization Science, Vol. 2, No. 1 (1991)
  • Algorithms to Live By — Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths (2016)
02-Systems/adjacent-possible.md:
References

The concept of the adjacent possible was coined by theoretical biologist Stuart Kauffman to describe the boundary of what can emerge from a given state. Steven Johnson extended it as a framework for understanding innovation.

  • Where Good Ideas Come From — Steven Johnson (2010)
  • The Origins of Order — Stuart A. Kauffman (1993)
06-Startups/design-thinking.md:
References

Herbert Simon introduced design as a 'science of the artificial' (1969). The modern human-centered design process was developed by IDEO (David Kelley, Tim Brown) and the Stanford d.school.

  • Change by Design — Tim Brown (2009)
  • The Design of Everyday Things — Don Norman (1988; revised 2013)
  • Creative Confidence — Tom Kelley & David Kelley (2013)
06-Startups/crossing-the-chasm.md:
References

Developed by Geoffrey A. Moore, building on Everett Rogers's diffusion of innovations curve. First published in 1991, revised and expanded in 2014.

  • Crossing the Chasm — Geoffrey A. Moore (1991; 3rd ed. 2014)
  • Inside the Tornado — Geoffrey A. Moore (1995)
  • Diffusion of Innovations — Everett M. Rogers (1962; 5th ed. 2003)
07-Business/disruptive-innovation.md:
References

The theory of disruptive innovation was developed by Clayton M. Christensen, introduced in a 1995 paper with Joseph Bower in the Harvard Business Review and fully elaborated in The Innovator's Dilemma.

  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
  • The Innovator's Solution — Clayton M. Christensen & Michael E. Raynor (2003)
07-Business/three-horizons.md:
References

Developed by Mehrdad Baghai, Stephen Coley, and David White at McKinsey & Company, introduced in The Alchemy of Growth (1999). Widely adopted in corporate strategy and innovation planning.

  • The Alchemy of Growth — Mehrdad Baghai, Stephen Coley & David White (1999)
  • The Innovator's Dilemma — Clayton M. Christensen (1997)
10-Learning/deep-work.md:
References

Deliberate practice research by K. Anders Ericsson established the ~4-hour performance ceiling for elite performers. Cal Newport synthesized this into practical guidance for knowledge workers. Daniel Kahneman's System 2 framework explains the underlying depletion mechanism.

  • Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World — Cal Newport (2016)
  • The Cambridge Handbook of Expertise and Expert Performance — K. Anders Ericsson et al., eds. (2006)
  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
05-Psychology/planning-fallacy.md:
References

Identified by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979. Reference class forecasting — the prescriptive remedy — was developed by Bent Flyvbjerg. Kahneman's inside view / outside view framework provides the explanatory structure.

  • Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
  • Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases — Science Vol. 185 — Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky (1974)
  • Megaprojects and Risk: An Anatomy of Ambition — Bent Flyvbjerg, Nils Bruzelius & Werner Rothengatter (2003)
07-Business/makers-schedule.md:
References

Paul Graham articulated the maker/manager schedule distinction in a 2009 essay. Gloria Mark's cognitive science research quantified the interruption re-focus cost. Cal Newport provides the complementary deep work framework.

  • Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule — Paul Graham (paulgraham.com, July 2009)
  • The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress — CHI Proceedings — Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith & Ulrich Klocke (2008)
  • Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World — Cal Newport (2016)
11-Leadership/mission-command.md:
References

Mission Command is rooted in Prussian military doctrine formalised by Helmuth von Moltke the Elder (1800–1891). It was codified for modern organisations by Stephen Bungay.

The Art of Action — Stephen Bungay, 2011

Moltke on the Art of War: Selected Writings — Helmuth von Moltke / Daniel Hughes ed., 1993

Turn the Ship Around! — L. David Marquet, 2013
11-Leadership/ooda-loop.md:
References

The OODA Loop was developed by John Boyd (1927–1997), US Air Force Colonel and military strategist, through his unpublished briefings "Patterns of Conflict" and "A Discourse on Winning and Losing."

boyd: The Fighter Pilot Who Changed the Art of War — Robert Coram, 2002

The Art of Maneuver — Robert Leonhard, 1991

Certain to Win — Chet Richards, 2004
04-Economics/goodharts-law.md:
References

Charles Goodhart first described the principle in a 1975 Bank of England paper on monetary policy. Marilyn Strathern's 1997 generalisation is the canonical academic formulation.

The Tyranny of Metrics — Jerry Z. Muller, 2018

Measuring and Managing Performance in Organizations — Robert Austin, 1996
04-Economics/principal-agent-problem.md:
References

The formal economic treatment was developed by Michael Jensen and William Meckling in their landmark 1976 paper on managerial behaviour, agency costs and ownership structure.

The Handbook of Organizational Economics — Gibbons & Roberts eds., 2013

Predictably Irrational — Dan Ariely, 2008
01-General-Thinking/cynefin-framework.md:
References

The Cynefin Framework was developed by Dave Snowden while at IBM Global Services in 1999, and has been refined through subsequent academic and practitioner work.

Cynefin: Weaving Sense-Making into the Fabric of Our World — Dave Snowden et al., 2020

The Fifth Discipline — Peter Senge, 1990
07-Business/scenario-planning.md:
References

Scenario Planning was developed at Shell in the 1970s by Pierre Wack and Ted Newland, building on earlier work by Herman Kahn at RAND. Peter Schwartz later codified the methodology for general business use.

The Art of the Long View — Peter Schwartz, 1991

Scenarios: The Art of Strategic Conversation — Kees van der Heijden, 1996

The Living Company — Arie de Geus, 1997
11-Leadership/organizational-culture.md:
References

Edgar Schein (1928–2023) developed his three-level model of culture while Professor of Management at MIT Sloan School of Management, through decades of consulting and organisational research.

Organizational Culture and Leadership — Edgar Schein, 1985 (5th ed. 2017)

The Corporate Culture Survival Guide — Edgar Schein, 1999

An Everyone Culture — Robert Kegan & Lisa Laskow Lahey, 2016
11-Leadership/change-management.md:
References

The field was shaped by Kurt Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze model (1947), John Kotter's 8-step framework (1996), and Prosci's ADKAR model developed by Jeff Hiatt (1998).

Leading Change — John Kotter, 1996

ADKAR: A Model for Change in Business, Government and our Community — Jeff Hiatt, 2006

Managing Transitions — William Bridges, 2009
11-Leadership/risk-management.md:
References

Enterprise Risk Management was codified by COSO (Committee of Sponsoring Organisations) in 2004 and updated in 2017. ISO 31000 provides the international standard. The Three Lines of Defence model is maintained by the Institute of Internal Auditors.

Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance — COSO, 2017

Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk — Peter Bernstein, 1996

The Failure of Risk Management — Douglas Hubbard, 2009
07-Business/raci-framework.md:
References

The RACI model emerged from project management practice in the 1950s–1980s and was popularised through the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK) and consulting firm methodology.

Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) — Project Management Institute, 7th ed. 2021

The Responsible Manager — Robert Goffee & Gareth Jones, 2013

Organizational Design — Naomi Stanford, 2015
01-General-Thinking/theory-of-change.md:
References

Theory of Change emerged from evaluation theory in the 1990s, associated with Carol Weiss and the Aspen Institute Roundtable on Community Change. It has since been widely adopted in international development, philanthropy, and corporate strategy.

Realistic Evaluation — Ray Pawson & Nick Tilley, 1997

The Logic Model Guidebook — Lisa Wyatt Knowlton & Cynthia Phillips, 2013

Lean Impact — Ann Mei Chang, 2018
11-Leadership/board-governance.md:
References

Modern corporate governance was substantially shaped by the Cadbury Report (UK, 1992), Sarbanes-Oxley (US, 2002), and the King Reports (South Africa, 1994–2016). The OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (updated 2023) provide the international standard.

Corporate Governance — Robert Monks & Nell Minow, 5th ed. 2011

The Boardroom Imperative — Ram Charan, 2005

OECD Principles of Corporate Governance — OECD, 2023
12-Pre-built-Chains/transformation.md:
References

The Transformation Chain synthesises Kotter's 8-Step Change Model, Schein's organisational culture framework, COSO's ERM, and the RACI governance model into a sequenced executive protocol.

Leading Change — John Kotter, 1996

The Heart of Change — John Kotter & Dan Cohen, 2002

Organizational Culture and Leadership — Edgar Schein, 1985 (5th ed. 2017)
